title: Dark Portals
author: Michael Foster
summary: Michael Foster writes about the death of his friend Mark McClure from addiction and despair, reflecting on how some families have a gravitational pull toward self-destruction -- what he calls a 'dark portal' that tries to drag generation after generation back into itself. Foster traces his friendship with Mark through a Christian skateboard ministry, shared theological reading, and eventually Mark's marriage; he then chronicles Mark's long struggle with alcohol and its tragic conclusion after his wife Nicole's accidental death. The essay is both a grief narrative and a call for men who show up: who answer the phone, sit with the grieving, refuse to abandon friends in darkness. Foster argues that there are neighborhoods, towns, and pockets of America where despair hangs like thick fog, and that the battles happening there rarely make the news but are everywhere. The piece closes with a pastoral exhortation to give yourself to your people and places and love your neighbor.
points: The 'dark portal' metaphor captures how patterns of addiction, divorce, laziness, and despair can operate across generations like a gravitational pull -- you can spend years trying to put distance between yourself and it, and it never entirely stops calling your name.

Foster's observation that he and Mark both came from broken families and were 'trying to outrun something' frames addiction not as individual moral failure but as a generational force that requires sustained counter-effort to escape.

The essay lifts up Elliott Liske as a model of what men are called to do: answer the phone, show up, listen, encourage, and do the quiet work that rarely gets noticed but often means everything to a hurting man.

There are neighborhoods and pockets of America where despair hangs over people like thick fog -- addiction has hollowed out families, loneliness has become normal, and many have stopped believing a different future is possible -- but these battles have names and faces.
The lie despair tells is that nobody cares and that nothing will ever change -- and the counter to that lie is not argument but presence: men who refuse to let the darkness have the final word.
quotes: The best way I know to describe it is that some families seem to have a gravitational pull toward self-destruction. It is like a dark portal that keeps trying to drag generation after generation back into itself. You can feel it pulling at you.

Mark and I both came from broken families. His was probably more broken than mine. We were both trying to outrun something. We both knew there were patterns behind us that had swallowed up people we loved: addiction, divorce, laziness, despair.

In particular, my friend Elliott Liske poured himself out for Mark. Elliott loved him faithfully during one of the darkest periods of his life. He listened. He encouraged. He showed up. He prayed. He did the kind of quiet work that rarely gets noticed but often means everything to a hurting man.

There are neighborhoods, towns, and entire pockets of America where despair hangs over people like a thick fog. Addiction has hollowed out families. Loneliness has become normal. Men and women are haunted by their childhood into their adulthood.

These battles rarely make the news, but they are everywhere. They have names and faces. They are happening to people we grew up with, people we worshiped beside, people we shared meals with, people we loved.

If you are in that darkness right now, if despair feels like it is closing in around you, if addiction has convinced you that escape is impossible, please reach out to someone. Call a friend. Call your pastor. Walk into a church. Ask for help. Do not suffer alone.
We need more men like that. And we need to be more like that ourselves. Give yourself to your people and places. Love your neighbor.
